title: System Design Lab
intro: Drag components onto the canvas, connect them, then send virtual traffic through your design. Every design starts with $200,000 of virtual AWS credit, spent at the design's hourly cost while its traffic runs.
priceNote: Approximate AWS on-demand list prices for Mumbai, for learning only. Data transfer and storage are not counted yet.
modelNote: Capacities are rules of thumb for a typical web API, not benchmarks. The simulation shows each component's utilisation, the queueing delay it adds, and the requests it has to drop once it is past capacity. Traffic follows the Clients' pattern over the simulated day, so pick a faster speed to watch a whole day. Queues are asynchronous: users get their answer once the message is stored, and a backlog shows how far behind the workers are.
smallScreen: The Lab is built for a laptop or tablet. On a phone you can look around, but designing is easier on a bigger screen.

components.name: Clients
components.desc: Your users' apps and browsers. Set how many requests per second they send at the busiest moment, and how that changes through the day.

rps.label: Requests per second (at the busiest moment)

patterns.label: Lunch and dinner rush
patterns.desc: The full rate at 8:30 pm, three quarters of it at 1 pm, almost nothing at 4 am.

patterns.label: Flash sale at 8 pm
patterns.desc: The full rate for 15 minutes from 8 pm, a fifth of it the rest of the day.

patterns.label: IND vs PAK match night
patterns.desc: Quiet all day, a jump at the 7 pm toss, a dip at the innings break and the peak in the last over at 10:18 pm.

components.like: The crowd at the door: everyone who wants something from you, all at once.

components.name: CDN
components.desc: CloudFront. Servers in cities near your users keep copies of what they ask for (video chunks, images, menus) and answer from there; only what they don't have reaches your servers. Scales by itself and never crashes. Billed per request; data transfer is not counted in the Lab.
components.like: A kirana shop in every lane. Most things people need are already on its shelf; only rare items come all the way from the warehouse.

live.label: Live content: every chunk is new (live video)

components.name: API Gateway
components.desc: Managed front door: routing, authentication and throttling. Billed per request. Past its limit of about 10,000 requests a second it rejects the extra requests (429) but never crashes.
components.like: The security desk of an office building. It checks who you are, points you to the right floor, and stops letting people in when the lobby is full.

components.name: Load Balancer
components.desc: Application Load Balancer. Spreads requests evenly over the servers it points at and scales by itself. Cheaper than an API Gateway at high traffic, but it does no authentication or throttling. Billed per hour plus per LCU, a unit of load (here about 300 requests a second).
components.like: Booths at a toll plaza. Cars spread across every open booth, so no single lane jams.

components.name: Server
components.desc: EC2 instances running your API. More or bigger instances handle more requests a second. Each request makes a few database queries. With autoscaling on, the group adds instances when load rises and removes them when it falls.

autoscaling.label: Autoscaling
autoscaling.note: Keeps each instance near 60% load. A new instance takes 4 minutes to boot, so a sudden spike still hits the instances already running. Instances are removed after load has stayed low for 15 minutes. You pay for the instances that are running.
autoscaling.like: Opening more ticket counters at the station when the rush starts. It helps, but a new clerk takes a few minutes to sit down.

components.like: Cooks in a kitchen. Each one handles a few orders at a time; more cooks, or faster ones, handle a bigger rush.

components.name: Queue
components.desc: SQS standard queue. The sender is done as soon as the message is stored; the workers it points at take messages as fast as they can. If messages arrive faster than the workers handle them, a backlog builds up and drains later. Users never wait for the workers. Billed per request.
components.like: The token system at a bank. Customers take a token and wait; tellers call the next token when they are free.

components.name: Cache
components.desc: ElastiCache for Redis, placed between your servers and the database (Server → Cache → Database). Reads it already holds come back in about a millisecond; misses go on to the database, and so do writes, at once or later depending on the write policy. Every query touches the cache, so size it for the full query rate. After a restart it is empty and has to warm up again.

options.label: Write-through
options.desc: Each write goes to the cache and the database before the caller gets an answer. Slower writes, nothing lost if the cache crashes.

options.label: Write-back
options.desc: The cache answers at once and writes to the database later, as fast as the database has room. Fast writes, but if the cache crashes, writes it had not passed on yet are lost.

options.label: Send queries to the database
options.desc: What most code does when the cache errors: read and write the database directly. Nothing fails, but the database takes every query.

options.label: Fail the queries
options.desc: The requests that needed the cache fail until it is back. The database is protected.

components.like: The water bottle on your desk. It is one sip away, so you only walk to the kitchen when it is empty. Write-back is a shopkeeper noting sales in a notebook and copying them into the ledger later: quick, until the notebook is lost.

components.name: Database
components.desc: RDS for PostgreSQL. Every request that reaches a server makes that server's number of queries. Multi-AZ keeps a standby copy, fails over when the primary crashes, and doubles the price.
components.like: The shop's ledger: the one record everyone trusts, so every change has to be written into it carefully.

crashNote: Overloaded components can crash. A server group crashes after 10 simulated minutes above 150% of its capacity and restarts 5 minutes later (and crashes again if the load is still there). A database crashes after 5 minutes above 120%: with Multi-AZ the standby takes over in 2 minutes, without it the database is down for 30. The API Gateway never crashes; past its limit it rejects the extra requests. Clients retry a failed request once, which adds load. Crashed components are still billed. A cache crashes after 5 minutes above 150% and is back 10 minutes later, empty: its hits climb back over 10 minutes while the misses land on the database. While a cache is down its queries go to the database or fail, as set on the cache. Load Balancers and Queues scale by themselves and never crash.

challenges.title: Too much for one server
challenges.brief: Zotato's order API runs on one server, and 2,000 requests a second are arriving. Keep orders flowing for six hours.
challenges.hint: One server handles about 600 requests a second. Add instances, and check that the database can take the queries they send.

challenges.title: Lunch and dinner rush
challenges.brief: A full day of Zotato traffic: quiet at night, busy at lunch, busiest at 8:30 pm with 3,000 requests a second.
challenges.hint: Size for the dinner peak, or let autoscaling follow the day. Look at what the API Gateway costs at this traffic.

challenges.title: Survive IND vs PAK
challenges.brief: 3.5 crore people watch India play Pakistan live, all at once. Every viewer's player asks for a 4-second chunk of video every 4 seconds: 87.5 lakh requests a second in the last over. Keep the stream up from 7 pm to 11 pm.
challenges.hint: No server farm takes 87.5 lakh requests a second. A CDN answers 99 of every 100 near the viewers, so size your servers for the rest, at the last over. But this is live video: when your servers fail, every viewer buffers, and everyone arrives at the toss at once, faster than autoscaling can boot servers.

stars.label: At least 99% of video requests succeed over the evening
No buffering around the toss (7:05 to 7:35 pm): 99.95%
No buffering in the last over (10:10 to 10:35 pm): 99.95%

challenges.title: The 8 pm flash sale
challenges.brief: At 8 pm Zotato runs a 15-minute flash sale: 8,000 requests a second, five times the usual. Survive it.
challenges.hint: New instances take 4 minutes to boot and the sale lasts 15. Each request makes 2 database queries.

challenges.title: The menu everyone reads
challenges.brief: 5,000 people a second open restaurant menus. Each request makes 4 database queries, almost all reads.
challenges.hint: No database here takes 20,000 queries a second. A cache answers 85% of reads; only misses and writes reach the database.

challenges.title: The cache restarts at dinner
challenges.brief: At 8:15 pm, in the middle of the dinner rush, Zotato's cache crashes. When it comes back it is empty. Keep the database standing.
challenges.hint: While the cache is down, its queries go to the database, and for 10 minutes after it returns most still do. Size for that, or don't depend on one cache.

challenges.title: Don't lose an order
challenges.brief: Zotato's cache takes writes too (40% of queries are writes) and flushes them to the database later. Half an hour in, the cache crashes.
challenges.hint: Write-back is fast until the cache crashes with writes it has not passed on. What does write-through ask of the database?

import.title: Import your own architecture
import.intro: Type your system one chain per line, joining components with ->. The same name on two lines is the same component; add :name to tell two apart (Server:orders, Server:workers).
import.placeholder:
Clients 3000 rush -> Load Balancer -> Server:orders x4 auto up to 12 -> Cache 85% hits -> Database db.m5.large multi-az
Server:orders -> Queue -> Server:workers x2 -> Database
options: Clients: a number is requests a second; rush, sale or steady sets the pattern
Server: x4 instances, a size such as m5.large, auto up to 12, 3 queries
Database: a size such as m5.xlarge, multi-az
import.file: Or open a JSON file exported from the Lab
